title: Berdyaev and Shestov
keyWorks: L. Shestov, The Apotheosis of Groundlessness (All Things Are Possible) (1905)
N. Berdyaev, The Meaning of the Creative Act (1916)
N. Berdyaev, The Destiny of Man (1931)
N. Berdyaev, Self-Knowledge (Dream and Reality) (1949, posthumous)
summary: Nikolai Berdyaev (1874–1948) and Lev Shestov (1866–1938) were Russian philosophers and longtime friends who both ended up as émigrés in France. Berdyaev built a philosophy of freedom and creativity: a human being, he was convinced, is called not only to obey but to create something new. Shestov spent his life rebelling against the rule of "necessity" and of general truths that cannot hear the living, suffering person. Both were religious thinkers; their views are presented here as their own search, not as a doctrine you are asked to accept.
onEmotions: For both of them, feelings are not an obstacle to reason but the voice of a living person, which general explanations must not drown out. Berdyaev drew fine distinctions between fear and dread, between longing and boredom, and showed how fear, malice or habit can enslave a person, while freedom and creativity bring them back to themselves. The main danger, he believed, was "objectification": a living person turned into a thing, a role or a function, including in their own eyes. Shestov defended the suffering person's right to cry out, to protest and to disagree: he argued with any philosophy that teaches resignation to the inevitable, and saw in reason's "self-evident truths" not a consolation but a prison. Together they invite you to take your feelings seriously, as the truth of a person rather than a mistake to be corrected as quickly as possible.

anxiety.text: "Philosophy should not reassure people but unsettle them," Lev Shestov wrote. When anxiety knocks the ground out from under you, it is truly frightening, and he wouldn't pretend otherwise. He called one of his books The Apotheosis of Groundlessness: rather than soothing anxiety by sliding a ready-made system underneath it, he doubted that such firm ground exists at all. Berdyaev would add that uncertainty is the other side of freedom: where everything is settled in advance there is no anxiety, but there is no creativity either. From their point of view, anxiety is not a malfunction but the price of an open future. You don't have to defeat it; you can carefully bear it, the way you bear each step on an unfamiliar road.
anxiety.practice: Stand up and take a few slow steps around the room, feeling each one, as if on an unfamiliar road with no guarantees. Say to yourself: "I don't know how it will turn out, and still I walk."

fear.text: In 1920 Berdyaev was arrested by the Cheka, and at his interrogation by Dzerzhinsky himself he spent nearly an hour setting out his convictions, after which he was released. Fear is a strong and honest feeling; Berdyaev knew it, but he also knew how not to let it decide for him. Fear, for Berdyaev, is one of the main forces that make a person a slave: out of fear we submit, we hide, we give up our own freedom. But he did not call on anyone to "stop being afraid" by sheer willpower. He believed that inner freedom and a creative attitude to life gradually loosen fear's grip. Seen this way, your fear is no disgrace. But it is worth asking: what is it trying to make me submit to right now, and is there a step, however small, that is truly mine?
fear.practice: Imagine for a minute that fear has stepped aside and isn't deciding for you. What small step would you take then? Just look at it; you don't have to take it now.

sadness.text: "Oh that my grief were thoroughly weighed!" Shestov returned again and again to this cry of Job's and even called a book In Job's Balances. Sadness doesn't always need comforting; sometimes it needs to be heard. He spent his life arguing with philosophers who rush to explain suffering with general truths: "that's how the world works," "it is reasonable and necessary." In his books the voice of the suffering person, the biblical Job or Dostoevsky's underground man, matters more than any orderly system. Shestov believed sorrow has a truth of its own that reason has no right to cancel. Berdyaev wrote about toska, a longing that reaches toward something greater than everyday life. From their point of view, your sadness may not be a mistake that needs urgent fixing but a sign that you sense the depth of life and refuse to accept flat explanations.
sadness.practice: Speak your sadness aloud in a sentence or two, like Job, without explaining it or comforting yourself. Just let it sound in the room.

grief.text: "Socrates was poisoned": reason says this is an eternal truth that can never be undone, and Shestov refused all his life to make peace with it. Grief, too, does not accept comforts like "it was meant to happen." The main adversary in his philosophy is "necessity": the conviction that whatever has happened is reasonable and could not have been otherwise. In Athens and Jerusalem he argues with the whole tradition that teaches humble acceptance of the irreparable, and recalls the idea of the medieval theologian Peter Damian that nothing is impossible for God. For Shestov, a religious thinker, this was a hope beyond the reach of logic. You don't have to share his faith to hear his lesson: your protest against the loss is not immaturity but the voice of a love that will not consent. Grief may be allowed to disagree.
grief.practice: Say one sentence of disagreement aloud: "I do not accept that it had to be this way." Then sit in silence for a minute beside that disagreement, adding nothing.

loneliness.text: Berdyaev admitted that from childhood and all his life he felt a certain estrangement from the world around him: loneliness was his old companion. If you feel lonely now, he knew this feeling from the inside. He even devoted a book to the subject, Solitude and Society (in Russian, I and the World of Objects: An Essay in the Philosophy of Solitude and Communion). His idea is that loneliness is sharpest among people, when relationships turn into functions, roles and exchange, into what he called "objectification." What cures it is communion: the meeting of one person with another, of "I" with "Thou," where neither becomes an object for the other. So loneliness, for Berdyaev, says nothing about your inadequacy; it speaks of a person's longing for a real meeting. That is found not in the number of contacts but in a single genuine one.
loneliness.practice: Recall a person with whom you once had a real meeting, not a role but a conversation. Send them a few words, or simply recall that conversation in detail.

anger.text: "Twice two makes four is no longer life, gentlemen, but the beginning of death": Shestov loved these words of Dostoevsky's underground man. Anger is the energy of disagreement, and Shestov and Berdyaev treated rebellion with respect. Shestov rose up against "self-evident truths," the things everyone accepts as inevitable; the hero of Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground, whom he valued so highly, refuses to accept even "twice two makes four" if it crushes a living person. Berdyaev, too, saw protest as an expression of freedom. But he also warned that malice and hatred easily make a person a slave of the very one they are fighting. From their point of view, anger deserves to be acknowledged: it tells you that you disagree with something. Then ask yourself: how can I keep the strength of my disagreement without letting anger enslave me?
anger.practice: Press your palms against a wall and push with all your strength on the out-breath; feel the force of your "no." Then let go and say in one sentence what exactly you disagree with.

shame.text: One of the great misfortunes of human life, for Berdyaev, was "objectification": a living person turned into a thing, a label, an item on someone else's list. Shame arises precisely when we see ourselves through someone else's eyes, eyes that assess and condemn. But for Berdyaev a person can never be reduced to how they look from the outside. The person is a mystery; not a part of some whole, not an item on someone else's list. What matters most is the inner, free, creative core, which no outside judgment can exhaust or cancel. Shame, seen this way, shows that you have fallen under a gaze that turns you into a thing. You can acknowledge that gaze, and remember that you are more than what can be seen of you right now.
shame.practice: Look at your palm for a minute: the lines, the scars, the warmth. Say to yourself: "I am more than what can be seen of me right now."

guilt.text: Law, redemption, creativity: these were Berdyaev's three ethics, three ways of living with your own guilt, in The Destiny of Man. Guilt is heavy, and he thought carefully about what to do with it. The ethics of law judges actions by rules and easily turns into endless condemnation. The ethics of redemption, which grew out of Christianity, speaks of mercy and the possibility of forgiveness. The ethics of creativity sees a human being as someone able to create something new and so to answer the past with more than repentance. Berdyaev criticized the ethics of law because it can crush a person under the weight of guilt. Seen this way, guilt is a legitimate signal but not a final verdict. It can become not self-punishment but a creative response: what new thing can I do now?
guilt.practice: Do one small new thing today as your answer to what you feel guilty about: not punishment but creation, whether a kindness, a message, or a small thing put right.

envy.text: Berdyaev prized uniqueness so highly that comparing people at all seemed to him a small act of violence. Envy compares, and that hurts, yet comparison, for Berdyaev, is always a little untrue to a person. Comparison is only possible in the world of "objectification," where people become carriers of qualities, statuses and achievements, and there someone is always "higher." But creativity, which Berdyaev considered every person's calling, does not compete: each creates their own, and no one's gift takes another's place. Envy, seen this way, is a sign that you are looking at yourself as an object in a common queue. It can be turned into a question: what touched me in someone else's life, and what gift of my own does that point to?
envy.practice: Step outside for five minutes and watch something unrepeatable: one tree, one cloud, one face in the crowd. Ask yourself: what in my life is just as incomparable?

emptiness.text: Meaning does not lie ready-made in the world like a stone by the road: for Berdyaev, it is brought by a person's free creative act. When nothing inside responds, emptiness and apathy can be very heavy, and he knew these states and described them honestly. He believed that the world we usually live in, the world of "objectification," where everything has become objects, functions and duties, gives no meaning by itself: meaning, he was convinced, is born from a person's freedom and creativity. When the creative fire goes out, the world looks flat and grey. But emptiness, in his view, is not proof that there is no meaning; it is the experience of meaning's absence, and that experience itself speaks of a thirst for meaning. Even a tiny creative gesture is a first movement out of emptiness, not a duty to conquer it.
emptiness.practice: Do one small thing your own way, with no use and no judgment: draw a line on a page, move an object, hum a tune.

confusion.text: Shestov considered "self-evident truths" the sturdiest of prisons: you end up inside without noticing the walls. Confusion comes when the old answers have stopped working, and it is uncomfortable. Shestov thought this state is closer to the truth than it seems. All his life he argued with philosophical systems that promise to explain everything. In his view, real thinking begins where "self-evident truths" collapse, the things we had taken as beyond doubt. He often wrote his books in aphorisms and fragments rather than building them into a system: life, he believed, does not fit into a tidy order. Seen this way, confusion is not a sign of stupidity or weakness but a moment when you see the world without the ready-made scenery. Answers will come, but perhaps this time they will be your own answers rather than borrowed ones.
confusion.practice: Choose one "self-evident" thing you have started to doubt, and for a minute imagine that it is false. What opens up if so?

fatigue.text: In Slavery and Freedom Berdyaev drew up a whole catalogue of slaveries: to the state, to money, to public opinion, to one's own ideas about oneself. Tiredness and burnout are real, and he can help you see them more deeply. One of the least noticeable is when a person dissolves into functions and duties and becomes merely someone playing a role. Berdyaev called this "objectification": a living person turned into a mechanism. Such a life is draining even when there isn't all that much to do, because it leaves no room for freedom and creativity. Through this lens, burnout is not laziness but the resistance of a person who refuses to be nothing but a function. That tiredness deserves to be heard as a request for freedom.
fatigue.practice: Drop your shoulders, unclench your hands, and for a minute be not a function but simply a person sitting and breathing. Ask yourself: in which of my roles am I least myself right now?

boredom.text: Berdyaev insisted on separating longing from boredom, though people often confuse them. Boredom seems trivial, but he took it seriously. Longing, in his thinking, points upward: it is a yearning for something greater, for meaning, for another world, and there is movement in it. Boredom is when there is no movement: the world seems flat, finite, repetitive, as if there were nothing in it to wait for. In this light, boredom is not simply a lack of entertainment, and new entertainment does not cure it. You can try to turn it into longing, that is, to give it a direction. It's enough to ask yourself: what am I actually missing, what do I lack right now? Sometimes a very alive desire hides behind boredom.
boredom.practice: Imagine that your boredom is a longing that hasn't yet been given a direction. Ask yourself: what am I really missing? Name one word.

joy.text: On Sundays friends gathered at Berdyaev's house in Clamart, and the arguments over tea ran late into the evening: he valued the living joy of communion very highly. Joy can be accepted without reservations. He wrote about creative uplift, the state in which a person feels free and able to create something new. Joy, in his view, is a sign that at that moment the person is living from their freedom rather than from compulsion. Shestov, for all his focus on tragedy, also argued against the idea that reason has the right to take life's living gifts away in the name of "necessity" and "order." From their point of view, joy doesn't need to be justified, earned, or clouded by the thought that it will soon pass. It is a moment of real life in which you are more than a function or a duty.
joy.practice: Share your joy with one person, by phone or face to face, and notice how it sounds when someone else hears it.

love.text: In Self-Knowledge Berdyaev wrote with touching tenderness about his cat Murri: love, as he saw it, is always directed at the unrepeatable, not at "somebody." The tenderness you feel he considered one of the ways a person comes out of loneliness. In The Destiny of Man he wrote that love is directed at a concrete, unrepeatable person, not at their qualities or usefulness. To love, as he understood it, is to see in another their true image, the idea of them that runs deeper than their flaws. For Berdyaev, a Christian thinker, this image had a religious meaning; but his thought makes sense without faith too: love sees more in a person than others do. Tenderness is the response to that fragile uniqueness. Through this lens, your feeling is not naivety but a special kind of sight worth protecting.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and name aloud one trait that you see in them, and perhaps few others do.

gratitude.text: "Who was obliged to give you this?" Shestov would be glad to hear the answer "no one." Gratitude is the feeling that something has been given to you not by right or by law but as something extra. It follows that it is one of those experiences reason cannot fully explain. Reason looks for necessity: everything must be earned, derived, justified. Gratitude lives where something happens that no one was obliged to give. Shestov, a religious thinker, linked such a space with faith, for which "all things are possible," as opposed to the "Athens" of reason. Berdyaev would add that real gratitude is not servile: it is not a debt but a free response of the person. You can simply let yourself notice that some things in your life have been gifts.
gratitude.practice: Walk around your home or down the street and find one thing someone gave you though they didn't have to: a gift, some help, someone's work. Silently thank them.

hope.text: "With God nothing is impossible": Shestov repeated these words as if arguing with all of philosophy. Hope, for Shestov, is a revolt against the verdict "it cannot be otherwise." His main adversary is necessity: the conviction that the laws of reason and nature settle once and for all what is possible and what is not. In Athens and Jerusalem he set "Athens," the world of reason and inevitable truths, against "Jerusalem," biblical faith, for which, he was convinced, nothing is impossible. You don't have to share his faith; his thought matters without it: what seems inevitable today is not always the last word about the world. Berdyaev echoed him in his own way: freedom means the future is not decided in advance. Hope, in this light, is not naivety but faithfulness to the openness of life.
hope.practice: Name one "it cannot be otherwise" belief that holds you now, and for a minute imagine it is only a habit of thought. What becomes possible then?

nostalgia.text: In the autumn of 1922 Berdyaev stood on the deck of the "philosophers' ship" carrying expelled thinkers out of Russia, and he never went back. He knew nostalgia firsthand: he spent the rest of his life in emigration and near the end wrote a philosophical autobiography, Self-Knowledge. In it he observes that remembering is never a passive, exact reconstruction of the past: as we remember, we select, illuminate, transform. Berdyaev distinguished the time that carries things away and destroys them from an inner, "existential" time in which what we have lived through keeps its depth. Through this lens, nostalgia is not only a flight backward but also the creative work of memory: you are not simply losing the past, you keep giving it meaning. Whatever was genuine in it remains part of you.
nostalgia.practice: Do one thing "from back then" today: cook a dish, play a song, say aloud someone's favorite little phrase. Not to bring the past back, but to carry it on into the present.

craving.text: Berdyaev called himself a philosopher of freedom, and he would see a sharp craving as the place where freedom is being decided right now. There is nothing shameful in a sharp "I want it right now": that is how strong urges work. Berdyaev would say that at this moment two forces are arguing inside you. One is the urge, which demands things immediately and repeats the familiar loop. The other is the freedom of the person, which is able to pause. And he stressed that freedom is not given once and for all; it is carried out again and again. If yesterday went differently, today this freedom is still yours. A wave of craving rises and falls; every wave you wait out is a small act of freedom, not a feat of willpower.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, watch it for five minutes like weather outside the window: where it is in your body, whether it grows or weakens. Every wave you wait out is a small act of freedom.

addiction.text: A human being is greater than any of their falls: Berdyaev defended this idea against all the moralists. Addiction is a long loop, and he would be the last to call it a moral failure. He sharply criticized the "ethics of law," which only hands down verdicts. A person, for Berdyaev, never fully coincides with what happens to them: a core of freedom remains, even when life has been built around one single thing. Shestov would add a protest against a false "necessity": the thought "this is who I am, and it will never be different" is not a law of the universe but a verdict that can be contested. The way out of the loop is rarely walked alone: Berdyaev believed a person opens up in communion, in meeting others. Where you are understood without judgment, freedom returns more easily.
addiction.practice: Name to yourself one person or community, a mutual-help group for instance, where you would be understood without judgment. Berdyaev would call this "communion"; you don't need to decide anything now.

hangover.text: "How could you?" Berdyaev would recognize in this inner voice a judge he couldn't stand. The morning after can be hard: your body aches, and inside there's anxiety, shame, scraps of last night. Berdyaev would call this voice the "ethics of law," a morality that only judges and punishes. He believed such morality does not free a person but crushes them, and he set against it an ethics of mercy that sees a person as greater than their act. Shestov, for his part, argued all his life against the idea that the past decides once and for all, mercilessly, who we are. From their point of view, what matters now is not to pass sentence on yourself but to look after yourself: give yourself calm and rest. Working out what happened, and talking to people if you need to, can come later, more calmly.
hangover.practice: Say one sentence to yourself in a low voice, not as a judge but as a merciful friend: "You feel bad right now, so let's just rest first."

euphoria.text: Berdyaev knew creative ecstasy well, the moment when a person seems to break through the limits of the everyday world, and he did not consider such moments false. Right now, when euphoria has flared and every door seems open, he would rejoice with you. But he also described the "tragedy of creativity": the impulse reaches for the infinite, yet it takes shape in finite, limited things, and after the peak a cooling inevitably follows. Knowing this doesn't spoil the high; it makes it more honest. You can enjoy the sense of possibility without demanding that it last forever, and without rushing to turn every flash into big decisions. Let the uplift be a hint about what you want; you can bring it to life later, once things are calmer.
euphoria.practice: Write down in a word or two what seems so possible right now, and set the note aside for a few days: let the high point to a wish, and let decisions wait.

crash.text: Berdyaev called it the "tragedy of creativity": an inevitable rhythm in which every peak is followed by a cooling. The drop after a high hits hard: a moment ago everything seemed possible, and now it's all grey. The creative impulse, he wrote, strives toward a new world and a new life, but in the end it takes shape in finite things, a book, an event, a result, and after the peak comes a cooling. For him this was not proof that the impulse had been a deception but a feature of the human condition: we strive toward the infinite while living in the finite. Seen this way, the drop does not cancel what happened at the peak, and it doesn't mean you are "broken." It is the same wave in a different phase; there's no need to hurry the next rise.
crash.practice: Find with your eyes, or pick up, one thing that stayed with you after the high, however small. It is real, even though the rapture has passed.

panic.text: Berdyaev and Shestov wouldn't lecture you in a moment of panic: both knew that first you simply have to get through the wave. It is terrifying: a wave of dread washes over you, your heart pounds, your breathing goes ragged. A wave like this usually peaks and recedes within a few minutes. In his book on Kierkegaard, Shestov wrote about a dread that seizes a person and seems to paralyze their will; he did not regard it as weakness and saw in it one of the deepest human experiences. So in a moment of panic you don't need to decide, understand or conquer anything. It's enough to help your body ride out the wave, and let the dread be there without obeying it.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor, lay a palm on your chest, and breathe out longer than you breathe in. On each out-breath say to yourself: "This is a wave, and I don't obey it," until it begins to ebb.

dread.text: Fear is afraid of something concrete, while dread touches the ultimate questions of being: that is how Berdyaev told the two apart. The "what's the point of it all," the abyss, finitude, is a very heavy experience, and he considered it neither shameful nor a sickness. For Berdyaev, this dread is a sign of a person's depth, of the fact that they cannot be satisfied with a flat world. Shestov defended all his life the right to ask such questions and to refuse soothing answers. But neither saw dread as the last word: for Berdyaev the answer to the abyss was creativity and communion, bringing something new into the world and meeting others. You don't have to settle the question "what for" today; you can live with it without being left alone with it.
dread.practice: Don't stay alone with the question "why": say it aloud to someone close, or at least name to yourself one thing that was alive today, a person, a task, a moment.

fomo.text: Fashion, majority opinion, the standard of a "proper" life: Berdyaev spent his life defending the person against dissolving into all that. When it feels as if real life is happening somewhere else and you're missing it, it weighs on you. Berdyaev would call this the pressure of the "world of objectification," of general standards by which life is judged from the outside. A person, for Berdyaev, is unique, and their path cannot be compared with anyone else's, just as you can't compare two different poems by their number of lines. Seen this way, the only life you can miss is your own, not someone else's. The fear of missing out can become a useful question: what do I want, as opposed to the picture I've been shown?
fomo.practice: Put your phone away for ten minutes and do one thing that you yourself want, not the picture from the feed, however small.

sleepless.text: At night, Shestov would say, the daytime "self-evident truths," the familiar and reassuring ones, disappear, and the questions rise to their full height. Lying awake with your thoughts at three in the morning is agonizing: the mind spins and there are no answers. Shestov respected such questions and did not consider them an illness. But he also showed that a reason trying to settle them for good often just goes round in circles: the ultimate questions have no answer that can be derived like a theorem. Through this lens, night thoughts don't demand an immediate solution, and you don't have to defeat them. You can admit that the question is real, and set it aside, the way you set a heavy book aside until morning.
sleepless.practice: Lay your palm on your chest, breathe out slowly, and tell the night question: "You are real. We'll talk in the daytime." Set it aside the way you set down a heavy book until morning.

betrayal.text: The meeting of an "I" and a "thou," where neither becomes a means for the other, was for Berdyaev the most real thing that can happen between people. Betrayal hurts so much because you trusted not a function but a person. Betrayal is the moment you were turned into an object: an obstacle, a resource, a bargaining chip. Hence the particular pain: your very person has been wounded. But Berdyaev also insisted on something else: a person cannot be destroyed by being treated like a thing. That you were not seen speaks of the other's limits, not of your worth. As for forgiveness, from the standpoint of his philosophy of freedom, if it comes at all, it can only be a free act, never an obligation.
betrayal.practice: Say aloud: "I was treated like…, but I am…" and finish the second part the way you yourself know you are.

jealousy.text: To love a free person is not to own them: for Berdyaev this was almost an axiom. Jealousy is a mix of love, fear and pain, and it's hard not to feel it. The conclusion is simple: in jealousy love runs into the temptation of possession. He believed genuine love is directed toward a free person, and freedom cannot be appropriated: another human being cannot belong to us like a thing. Berdyaev wrote a great deal about how people become slaves of what they own or want to own. In this perspective, jealousy is the fear that the beloved's freedom will turn into loss. That fear is understandable. But it also contains a recognition that love is precious precisely because it is free: it is given, not held onto. You can let jealousy have its say and ask what it is really asking for: reassurance, attention, a conversation.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself what your jealousy is really asking for: reassurance, attention, a conversation? Think about how you might calmly ask for that directly.

resentment.text: Berdyaev would probably recognize in an old grievance a chain that binds a person to the one who hurt them. A grievance is a weight you carry for years, sometimes no longer remembering all the details. Through this lens, a grievance living inside you for a long time becomes one of the forms of slavery he wrote about: you end up tied to the person who hurt you and keep living in their shadow. At the same time, Berdyaev opposed any compulsion in spiritual life, and so also a forced "let it go and forgive." His answer lies rather in creativity: a life that builds something new gradually stops revolving around the wound. You can ask not "how do I forgive" but "what do I want to create in a life where this grievance is no longer the main thing."
resentment.practice: Take one small step today toward something you'd like to create that has nothing to do with the grievance: a sketch, a call, the first five minutes of something new.

heartbreak.text: Job sat in the ashes and refused his friends' explanations, and Shestov considered his cry more honest than all the consolations of philosophy. A broken heart is a pain that shouldn't be rushed. Shestov would side with your refusal to accept it: he believed philosophy too often teaches resignation, "these things happen, it's the law of life," and so drowns out the cry of a living person. Berdyaev, for his part, saw a tragic depth in love: it is directed at what is eternal in another person, yet lives in a fragile, finite world where meetings can end. From their point of view, your pain is not naivety or weakness but a measure of how real the love was. It doesn't need a quick explanation. You can allow yourself to grieve and to disagree.
heartbreak.practice: Say a few sentences aloud in the first person, like Job, with no explanations or conclusions, simply about how you are now. No one has to hear it but you.

impostor.text: No position, for Berdyaev, ever fully coincides with a living person: the role belongs to the world of "objectification," while the person is always more. When it feels as if any minute it will come out that you're not who people take you for, it wears you down. He distinguished the person from the social role. A role is a function in the world of "objectification," with its positions, ratings and expectations; a person is a living mystery that never fully coincides with any role. That's why anyone who looks at themselves honestly feels, in some sense, "not quite in their place": their inner life is larger and more complex than any job title. This is not deception but a sign that you are a person, not a function. Your doubt may mean not "I'm pretending" but "I'm more than how I'm seen from outside."
impostor.practice: Say two sentences aloud to yourself: "My role is…" and "But I am…", finishing the second not with a job title but with what truly matters to you.

self_hatred.text: A judge who passes sentence before the case is even heard: that is probably how Berdyaev would describe the inner critic. Self-hatred causes real pain, and you don't have to agree with that voice. Berdyaev would call it the voice of the "ethics of law," a morality that only judges, passes sentence and is never satisfied. He believed such an ethics can crush a person, and that it forgets the main thing: a person is not a sum of deeds and flaws but an unrepeatable image that runs deeper than any mistake. Shestov argued all his life with "general truths" that speak in everyone's name and cannot see the living person. The inner critic, too, speaks in general truths: "you always," "you never." But it doesn't know the whole of you. You are more than its verdict.
self_hatred.practice: Catch one of the critic's sentences with "always" or "never" in it and recall at least one exception. Name that exception aloud.

helplessness.text: Dostoevsky's underground man called impossibility a "stone wall," and Shestov refused all his life to accept that the wall has the last word. When it seems that nothing depends on you, it is exhausting. Shestov wrote a great deal about people in hopeless situations, about Job and the characters of Dostoevsky and Tolstoy, and never demanded that they "pull themselves together." He believed that even when a person is powerless to change something, they are not obliged to accept that powerlessness as the final truth about the world: refusing to agree with "necessity" is already an inner movement. Berdyaev would add that freedom is not only an outward possibility of action but an inner dimension of the person that circumstances cannot take away entirely. You keep the right to choose how you relate to what is happening.
helplessness.practice: Lay your palm on a wall and feel how hard it is: this is what is not in your power. Then name aloud one thing that remains in your power, if only how you relate to it.

procrastination.text: Every beginning, for Berdyaev, is a creative act: it brings into the world something that wasn't there before. When "I can't get started" drags on and on, it's a familiar torment, and he would explain it unexpectedly. Such a beginning always involves risk and freedom, so it's no wonder a person freezes in front of it. Berdyaev also wrote about the "tragedy of creativity": the idea is always bigger than its realization, and whatever comes out will inevitably be more modest than what you imagined. Perhaps you're holding back precisely because you sense that gap in advance. But the gap can't be removed, and it says nothing about your inability. You can allow yourself an imperfect beginning; humans never get any other kind.
procrastination.practice: Start with a "bad" draft: spend five minutes on the first step, giving it permission in advance to be imperfect.

uprooted.text: Many years before emigrating, Shestov titled a book The Apotheosis of Groundlessness, as if foreseeing a life without ground. Later both thinkers lived through being torn from home themselves. In 1922 Berdyaev was expelled from Soviet Russia on the so-called "philosophers' ship," and afterwards lived near Paris. Shestov emigrated in the early 1920s and also settled in France. "Groundlessness" was for him not only a misfortune but also the honest position of a thinking person who doesn't lean on ready-made foundations. Losing your ground is painful, and it can be mourned. But, from their point of view, a person can live and think without firm ground underfoot, finding support in freedom, in friendship (they themselves were friends for decades), in their work.
uprooted.practice: Call one person today with whom you've stayed in touch despite the distance: this is your "portable ground." Berdyaev and Shestov held on to such a friendship for decades.

overload.text: Long before the endless feed, Berdyaev described the "world of objectification," where everything turns into the external: objects, facts, functions, streams. Overload from information noise is a legitimate tiredness, and he would recognize something familiar in it. In such a world a person lives more and more outwardly and less and less inside themselves. An endless feed is an almost perfect picture of that world: a stream of objects in which the living person gets lost. Berdyaev believed the real life of a person comes from within, from freedom, reflection, creativity, communion. When there's too much of the outer, no room is left for the inner. In this light, overload is not your inability to "cope" but the resistance of a person asking to come back to themselves.
overload.practice: Put your phone down, close your eyes, and for a minute listen to what you yourself think, not the feed. If one thought of your own arrives, that's enough.

unreality.text: Sometimes the familiar world suddenly looks like cardboard scenery, and a person gets frightened. Berdyaev would not call this madness: he himself believed that the world of objects, roles and functions is not the deepest reality. The feeling is unsettling and disorienting, and it deserves to be spoken of gently. But Berdyaev knew where to look for what is truly real: in the living person, in freedom, in communion, the meeting of "I" and "Thou." For him the most real thing was not the abstract but the concrete: this person, this feeling, this conversation. Seen this way, when the world feels unreal, you can lean on what is closest and most alive: a voice, a touch, a meeting.
unreality.practice: Touch something warm or rough and name the sensation in one word. Then call someone close and simply listen to their voice.

awe.text: What if the world of objects is only the surface? Berdyaev and Shestov asked this in earnest, and awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare gift you want to make last. Berdyaev would call it a moment when a person breaks through the familiar world of objects toward something greater, toward what he called the world of spirit. For him, a religious thinker, such moments were connected with God; but the experience he describes is familiar to non-believers too: the sense that reality is deeper than it usually appears. What Shestov valued in life was precisely what doesn't fit reason's calculations: the unexpected, the improbable, the miraculous. From their point of view, your awe doesn't need to be explained or reduced to something simple. It is a window that opened for a moment. You can simply stand by it for a while.
awe.practice: Stay in this feeling a minute longer without naming or explaining it; simply stand at the window that has opened.

relief.text: All his life Shestov argued with "necessity," the conviction that bad things are inevitable and everything is settled in advance. Relief feels like a hand that was gripping you has let go, and he would understand this feeling from the inside. Relief is a small refutation of that conviction: what you feared didn't happen, happened differently, or simply let go. In moments like these you can see that the world is not as closed as it seemed while you were anxious. Berdyaev would see in relief a moment of liberation: a person held in fear's grip breathes freely again. From their point of view, you don't need to hurry to replace relief with a new worry. It reminds you that the future is open, and that openness holds good things too.
relief.practice: Unclench your fists, open your palms and breathe out slowly. Say to yourself: "I was afraid that…, but it turned out…", and let your hands stay open.

calm.text: "Man is the point of intersection of two worlds," Berdyaev wrote in The Meaning of the Creative Act, and in stillness, he believed, the second of them becomes easier to hear. Calm and peacefulness are things you just want to live in. Berdyaev, for all his restless temperament, knew the value of inner quiet. He believed the real life of a person comes from within, from the depth of the spirit, not from the outer bustle of the world of objects. Calm, seen this way, is not inaction but a moment when a person is enslaved neither by fear, nor by haste, nor by other people's expectations. It is one of the forms of freedom: nothing is ordering you around right now. You don't need to do anything with this feeling; it's enough to stay in it.
calm.practice: Sit still for a minute and name to yourself what has no power over you right now: hurry, other people's expectations, fear. Simply note this freedom.

inspiration.text: Berdyaev gave The Meaning of the Creative Act the subtitle An Essay in the Justification of Man: a human being, he was convinced, is called not only to obey laws and atone for guilt but to create. The inspiration you feel now is one of his central themes. Creativity, for Berdyaev, continues the creation of the world, bringing into it what was not there before; for him, a Christian thinker, it was the human response to God's idea of that person. But even outside a religious context his thought is encouraging: your inspiration is not a whim but an expression of the deepest thing in you, your freedom. Berdyaev also knew the "tragedy of creativity": the realization is always more modest than the impulse. That's no reason to wait for perfection; it's a reason to begin.
inspiration.practice: Write down the first, rawest form of what inspires you, without improving it. Let the impulse leave a trace before the critic gets hold of it.

schadenfreude.text: Shestov saw Dostoevsky's "underground" not as a swamp but as truth: the place where a person finally stops pretending. Schadenfreude is one of those feelings that are embarrassing to admit even to yourself. He especially valued Dostoevsky for daring to show the "underground" movements of the soul, what people usually hide behind respectable words. Taking this thought further, honestly noticing schadenfreude in yourself is not a fall but a step toward a living truth about yourself. Berdyaev would add something else: a person is not reducible to individual movements of the soul; they are larger than those and free in how they respond to them. Schadenfreude can tell you about your tiredness, hurt or rivalry. But it doesn't define who you are or what you will do next.
schadenfreude.practice: Write down one honest sentence: "Someone else's failure made me feel better because…", without excusing or scolding yourself. Shestov would call this a step toward living truth.

contempt.text: "Stupid," "weak," "empty": Berdyaev would see in such labels a small prison both for the one labeled and for the one who labels. Contempt arises when another person seems lower, smaller, less worthy. He wrote about "objectification," turning a living person into an object, a function, a label. For him this is one of the main forms of slavery, both for the one who is objectified and for the one who objectifies. Contempt is exactly this kind of objectification: the other person becomes "that sort" for you, stupid, weak, empty, and stops being a mystery. Berdyaev insisted that every person is unique and cannot be reduced to their deeds or their social role. But contempt closes the door, while recognizing the person leaves it ajar, above all for you yourself.
contempt.practice: Name to yourself one thing about this person that you don't and can't know, such as their childhood or their thoughts at night. Notice whether the contempt shifts.

disgust.text: Berdyaev could not stand the "bourgeois spirit," a sated, frozen way of life in which everything alive has turned into habit and calculation. Disgust, at people, at a situation, sometimes at yourself, can be sudden and strong. In his autobiography Self-Knowledge, he admitted that all his life he felt a sense of estrangement from the world: much of everyday life seemed heavy, oppressive, repellent to him. In his view, the world of "objectification," of frozen forms, rules and conventions, really can repel a living person. Disgust is often directed not at people as such but at what has frozen in them, gone dead, become mechanical. Through this lens, disgust is a signal of longing for what is alive. Instead of suppressing it, you can ask: what genuine, free, living thing am I missing right now?
disgust.practice: Turn your eyes away from what disgusts you and find something alive and real nearby: a plant, a face, the light. Look at it for a minute.

revenge.text: Berdyaev lived through revolution and civil war and saw how revenge gives birth to new revenge until no one remembers how it began. The wish for revenge is a natural response to pain inflicted on you. He criticized the "ethics of law," in which justice comes down to retribution, and observed with unexpected bluntness that behind the wish to punish the guilty, "good" people often hide a thirst for revenge, an almost vindictive pleasure. Berdyaev believed retribution keeps a person enslaved to the evil done to them: you go on living by its rules. Against this he set the "ethics of creativity," in which a person answers evil not by repeating it but by creating something new. But you can act from freedom: protect yourself, name the injustice, without becoming what you are rising up against.
revenge.practice: Imagine answering not with revenge but with something new and free: protection, a clear word, walking away, creating something of your own. Which option gives you more air?

anger_at_loved.text: From his youth Berdyaev resisted narrow frames: those of the gentry, of family expectations, of propriety. Getting angry with the people closest to you, a partner, parents, children, and then feeling ashamed of it is very human. Later, in Slavery and Freedom, he wrote that a person can end up enslaved to the family and the roles it imposes: "the good son," "the patient mother," "the dependable partner." When a role presses too hard, the living person inside resists, and that resistance often breaks out as anger. In other words, anger at loved ones is often aimed not at the people themselves but at the tightness of the roles you have both ended up in. You can acknowledge the anger, and find a form for it that doesn't wound the people you love.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, pause for three breaths and silently name the role that is pressing on you: "I'm not angry at you, but at having to be…"

ambivalence.text: "Man is broad, too broad even; I'd have him narrower," says Mitya Karamazov, and Berdyaev considered this breadth Dostoevsky's great discovery. Loving someone close to you and at the same time not being able to stand them is a contradiction that's hard to bear. Berdyaev in general considered Dostoevsky the greatest expert on human contradictions. In Dostoevsky: An Interpretation (Dostoevsky's Worldview) he wrote that Dostoevsky showed the human being as polar, torn by opposing forces: in his characters love can be intertwined with hatred, tenderness with tormenting. Berdyaev saw nothing monstrous in this; for him it was a sign of the depth and freedom of human nature. Taking this thought further, mixed feelings are not proof that there is no love. The contradiction doesn't have to be resolved; it can be accepted as part of a living, complicated love.
ambivalence.practice: Say aloud one sentence that holds both love and difficulty, without a "but": "I love you, and it is very hard for me with you." Listen to how it sounds.

quote.text: Man is broad, even too broad; I would narrow him down.
quote.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
quote.source: The Brothers Karamazov (1880), words of Dmitri Karamazov

guilty_relief.text: "You mustn't feel that way": Berdyaev would recognize in this phrase the "ethics of law," ready to condemn any feeling that doesn't fit the general rule. Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a loved one who had been ill for a long time is often hidden deep inside. Lev Shestov rebelled all his life against "general truths" that cannot hear the concrete, suffering person. The conclusion is simple: relief is a living feeling of a living person who carried a weight for a long time. Moralizing demands that you feel nothing but sorrow, but a real soul is more complex than rules. Berdyaev believed a person's freedom includes the right to be honest with oneself, even when one's feelings don't match what is expected. Relief and love can exist at the same time.
guilty_relief.practice: Sit in silence and whisper to yourself: "I feel lighter. And that doesn't cancel my love." Stay with these words for a minute.

indifference.text: Shestov defended a living person's right not to conform to general norms, even in their own feelings. Sometimes where something "ought" to move you, it's quiet inside, and that feels unsettling. Berdyaev criticized the "ethics of law," which prescribes not only actions but feelings: here you're supposed to grieve, here to feel compassion. He believed a genuine feeling cannot be summoned on command: it is born of freedom, not of obligation. Through this lens, indifference is not always coldness. Sometimes it's tiredness, sometimes protection from something too strong, sometimes simply a pause after which the feeling will come by itself. Lev Shestov would add that a living person is not obliged to conform to general norms even in what they feel. You can admit, "Right now I don't feel what's expected of me," and not judge yourself for it.
indifference.practice: Honestly name to yourself what you feel instead of what you "should," even if it's "nothing" or "tiredness." Don't correct it; just acknowledge it.

escape.text: From the gentry, from Marxism, from many philosophical and church circles, Berdyaev kept leaving for somewhere freer all his life, and he admitted he never felt fully "one of them" anywhere. The urge to drop everything, the job, the city, the role, can be very strong. His main theme is freedom, and the main threat to freedom is slavery to society, the state, the family, a role. It follows that the urge to escape is the voice of a freedom that feels caged. But Berdyaev distinguished "freedom from," the wish to break out, and "freedom for," the wish to create something new. The first without the second only swaps one cage for another. You can ask yourself not only what you are running from, but also what you want to create.
escape.practice: Say two sentences aloud: "I want to be free from…" and "I want freedom in order to…", and listen to which one sounds stronger.

forbidden_attraction.text: Already in his early essay "The Metaphysics of Sex and Love," Berdyaev argued that eros is a mysterious creative force that doesn't fit accepted frameworks. Attraction to someone who is unavailable or "not right" can be strong and tormenting. Following Plato, Berdyaev saw in eros a longing for wholeness, a striving for a fullness that a person lacks. In other words, a forbidden attraction speaks not only of a particular person but of your deep thirst for fullness, aliveness, recognition. Berdyaev gave no recipes and passed no quick verdicts. But he invited us to look closely at desire: what is it really calling the soul toward?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Walk for five minutes and ask yourself, without naming anyone: "What quality of life stands behind this attraction: aliveness, fullness, being recognized?" Name one word.

social_anxiety.text: Whom do you see among people: spectators or companions? For Berdyaev this was the decisive question, and fear of people and their judgment can squeeze you from the inside. He wrote about "objectification": in society a person turns into an object, someone's assessment, a label, a role. Under others' gaze we feel like a thing being examined and rated. Taking this thought further, social anxiety is the fear of being objectified, reduced to what people will think of us. But Berdyaev insisted that a person is never reducible to an object. A person is a mystery no assessment can exhaust. He distinguished communion, a living meeting of two persons, from impersonal "society," where everyone rates everyone. Anxiety belongs to the second. Sometimes it helps to look among people not for an audience but for at least one conversation partner with whom a real meeting is possible.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next gathering, find one person with your eyes whom you could really talk to, and address yourself to them first.

uncertainty.text: "All things are possible to him that believeth": Shestov set these Gospel words against all the wisdom of reason, for which much is impossible once and for all. Uncertainty is hard: the future is unknown and you can't lean on it. For him uncertainty was not only a threat but also an openness: where nothing is predetermined, there is room for the unexpected, for what no logic would have predicted. Berdyaev, too, saw the future not as a finished script but as a space of freedom where a person takes part in creating something new. The conclusion is simple: uncertainty is the other side of freedom. But not knowing the future also means it isn't closed yet. You can allow yourself not to know, and still notice that you are able to influence it.
uncertainty.practice: Take one small action today that shapes the future even a little: a call, a question, a first step. Not knowing doesn't stop you from taking part.

waiting.text: The future, for Berdyaev, is not something you wait for like a train at a station: you take part in it and create it. Waiting, for an answer, for results, for news, can be agonizing. Shestov wrote a great deal about the biblical Job, who lost everything and waited for an answer: not consolation from his friends but a real answer to his cry. Shestov valued Job for refusing ready-made explanations and continuing to demand a living answer. Through this lens, waiting is a legitimate state in which you don't need to pretend to be calm. Like Job, you can honestly admit your impatience. And, as Berdyaev advised, you can refuse to hand your whole life over to waiting: while you wait, you are still able to create in the present.
waiting.practice: Say it aloud, honestly, like Job: "Waiting is hard for me." Then choose one small creative task for the next hour.

regret.text: Can God make what has been not to have been? Shestov took this medieval dispute seriously and sided with the living person for whom the past's final verdict is unbearable. Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again. In Athens and Jerusalem, Shestov boldly rebelled against the idea that the past is final and irrevocable, against what he called the power of necessity over human beings. Berdyaev came at it from another side: in the "ethics of creativity" a person answers mistakes not only with repentance but by creating something new. It follows that the past does not have the last word on who you will become. Regret is legitimate. But it can become not a verdict but the start of a new response.
regret.practice: Choose one small action that will be your new answer to what you regret, and do it today or set a time for it.

longing.text: "Not just anyone, but precisely this one": Berdyaev's whole philosophy of the person could fit into these words. Longing for a particular person is the ache for someone no one else can replace. Berdyaev built his philosophy on the idea of the person: unique, unrepeatable, not reducible to anything general. For him every human being is a whole world, and no general category exhausts them. Through this lens, longing for a particular person is a recognition of their uniqueness: what you miss is not "somebody" but precisely them. Berdyaev also wrote a lot about longing itself: in Self-Knowledge he confessed that this feeling accompanied him all his life, and he saw in it a sign that the soul reaches for something greater than the everyday. Longing does not cancel love; it bears witness to it. You can live through it as faithfulness to the unrepeatable meeting you had.
longing.practice: Recall three traits this person alone has and say them aloud, like names. Let yourself simply remember them.

world_pain.text: "Bread for myself is a material question; bread for my neighbor is a spiritual one," Berdyaev wrote. Pain for the world, from grim news, war, injustice, can be enormous. Berdyaev and Shestov, who lived through war, revolution and exile, knew this feeling. Berdyaev often recalled Ivan Karamazov's question in Dostoevsky: can one accept a world harmony built on the suffering of even one child? Berdyaev believed the suffering of a single person cannot be justified by any general goal. Shestov rebelled against every explanation that makes another's pain "necessary." Taking this thought further, your pain for the world is faithfulness to the value of every human being. You don't need to be ashamed of it or to muffle it. But you can give it a direction: into compassion, help, a creative response, without letting it destroy you.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete small way to answer what hurts, whether help, a donation, or a kind word to someone nearby; do it, and allow yourself to stop.

rejection.text: Vox clamantis in deserto, "a voice crying in the wilderness": Shestov gave this subtitle to his book on Kierkegaard, and it could have been the motto of his whole life. Rejection hurts: you weren't accepted, weren't chosen, weren't wanted. Shestov wrote for decades understood by few; many found his thought strange, awkward and too sharp. He took the side of those rejected by "general truths," the criteria by which the world decides who is needed and who isn't. Berdyaev added that a person is defined neither by public recognition nor by anyone else's judgment: a person is deeper and freer than any label. The conclusion is simple: rejection is someone's assessment, not the final truth about you. The pain of it is real. But it doesn't have to become your own verdict on yourself.
rejection.practice: Declare, like Job: "I was rejected, but I don't accept that…", and finish the sentence with the part of someone else's verdict you refuse to take on.

abandonment.text: Precisely because each person is unique, Berdyaev wrote in Solitude and Society, in some way they are always alone. The fear of being abandoned is a deep fear of being left alone, and Berdyaev never tried to mock it. But Berdyaev didn't stop there. He distinguished a loneliness that no outward company can overcome from genuine communion, the meeting of two persons, "I" and "Thou." Such communion doesn't guarantee that someone will stay forever, but it makes the bond alive. Through this lens, the fear of abandonment is a sign of a deep need for communion. That need can't be satisfied by controlling the other person. But it can be nourished, through meetings in which you are seen as a person.
abandonment.practice: Tell one person today that you value them, not to hold on to them but to make the meeting more alive. This is "communion" as Berdyaev meant it.

unrequited.text: Love, for Berdyaev, can't be earned, forced or bought: that is its freedom and its pain. When love goes unanswered, it wounds very deeply. For him love is a creative act that sees in another an unrepeatable person. But this freedom also holds pain: the other is free too, and may not respond. It follows that unrequited love was not a mistake. You saw the other's unrepeatable face, and that seeing was a genuine creative act. Berdyaev never promised that love would be mutual. But he believed the creative act of love itself is not lost: it changes the one who loves and stays in them. Your capacity to love so deeply is not a weakness but evidence of your freedom.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has opened in you: what tenderness, what strength you discovered in yourself. It will stay with you.

humiliation.text: One of Dostoevsky's novels is titled Humiliated and Insulted, and Berdyaev and Shestov both wrote a lot about how he portrayed such people. Humiliation wounds deeply, as if your dignity had been taken away. In Notes from Underground the humiliated hero grows bitter, and his hurt turns into malice. Shestov saw in the "underground man" the truth of a protest against a world that crushes the living person. In Dostoevsky: An Interpretation, Berdyaev stressed that every human being, even a humiliated one, has the dignity of a person that no one can take away. In other words, humiliation is a wound that can't be denied. But it speaks of violence done to you, not of your worth. You can acknowledge the pain and refuse to accept the other's view of you.
humiliation.practice: Stand up straight, feel the ground under your feet, and say to yourself: "I was humiliated, but there remains in me…" Name one thing no one can take from you.

body_shame.text: Berdyaev found the face the most expressive thing in a human being: in it, he thought, the person itself shows through. Being unhappy with your body can be a heavy background to life. Berdyaev argued with the tradition that separates soul from body and treats the body as something lower. For him the person is a wholeness: spirit, soul and body together. He stressed that the body is not just a shell but part of the image of the person, its expression in the world. Taking this thought further, body shame is often born of "objectification": we look at ourselves as an object to be rated and compared with a norm. Your body is not an exhibit to be graded but part of your uniqueness, of how you are present in the world. It doesn't have to meet a standard to be yours.
body_shame.practice: Look at your face in the mirror for one minute, not as an assessor but as someone greeting a familiar person. What do you see?

illness.text: "Don't explain my pain to me; hear it": that is probably how Job would sound in Shestov's retelling. Illness, when your body lets you down, can take away your strength, your plans, your familiar sense of yourself. Shestov wrote a great deal about the biblical Job, who lost everything, his health included, and was covered in sores. His friends came to comfort him and began explaining why it had happened, as if the misfortune followed a rule. Job refused to accept their explanations. Shestov saw a great truth in this: a suffering person is not obliged to agree that their pain is "right" or "deserved." The conclusion is simple: you don't need to look for meaning or blame in your illness. You can speak honestly about your pain and protest against it.
illness.practice: Tell one person honestly how you feel, and ask them not to give advice but simply to listen. Shestov would call this the right to your own voice.

pride.text: "This didn't exist, and now it does": Berdyaev considered this simple thought almost the most important one in a human life. Pride in what you've done is a healthy feeling, and you can enjoy it. In The Meaning of the Creative Act he argued that human beings are called to create, to continue the creation of the world by making what was not there before. For him creativity wasn't limited to art: a job well done, a solution found, a garden grown are creative acts too. At the same time, Berdyaev distinguished creative dignity from vainglory: vainglory closes in on itself and compares itself with others, while creative joy is directed at what has been made and at the world. Through this lens, healthy pride is the joy of having taken part in creation. You can enjoy that calmly, without apologizing and without comparing.
pride.practice: Put what you've made in front of you, or show it to one person, and look at it for a minute: you have added to the world something that wasn't there.

melancholy.text: All his life, Berdyaev admitted in Self-Knowledge, he was accompanied by longing, and he saw in it a sign of the soul's depth, not an illness. Bright sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow and tenderness are intertwined. He distinguished longing, fear and boredom. Boredom, he observed, pulls downward, toward emptiness, while longing, on the contrary, is turned upward: it is a yearning for something higher, for something greater than the everyday. It follows that melancholy is not a defeat but a sensitivity to the fact that the world is not exhausted by everyday life. This sadness says that there lives in you a striving toward something greater: beauty, meaning, the eternal. It doesn't need to be treated or chased away. You can live bright sadness as a quiet reminder of your depth.
melancholy.practice: Go to the window and look at the sky for a minute, asking yourself: "What, beyond my everyday life, is my soul longing for right now?" You don't need an answer.
